topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The federal Fair Housing Act, originally enacted as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, is codified in the United States Code at:
choice_a: 15 U.S.C. § 1 et seq.
choice_b: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 et seq.
choice_c: 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.
choice_d: 12 U.S.C. § 2601 et seq.
explanation: The Fair Housing Act is codified at 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq. (15 U.S.C. § 1 is the Sherman Antitrust Act; 42 U.S.C. § 1981/1982 are separate Reconstruction-era civil rights statutes; 12 U.S.C. § 2601 is RESPA.)
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq. (Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute); U.S. Dept. of Justice, Civil Rights Division, Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: As currently amended, the Fair Housing Act prohibits housing discrimination based on all of the following protected classes EXCEPT:
choice_a: Race or color
choice_b: Familial status
choice_c: Disability (handicap)
choice_d: Sexual orientation, as an explicitly named class in the statutory text
explanation: The seven classes explicitly named in the federal Fair Housing Act are race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not listed as separate protected classes in the statutory text itself (though HUD has interpreted sex discrimination to cover related claims in some contexts, and many states/localities add sexual orientation by their own law).
source_note: U.S. Dept. of Justice, Civil Rights Division, Fair Housing Act overview (justice.gov/crt/fair-housing-act-1).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: "Familial status," as a class protected by the federal Fair Housing Act, primarily protects:
choice_a: Families with one or more children under age 18, pregnant women, and persons in the process of securing legal custody of a minor
choice_b: Only married couples with children living in the household
choice_c: Any household of unrelated adults sharing a residence
choice_d: Households receiving public housing assistance
explanation: Familial status protects households that include a child under 18 who lives with a parent or legal custodian, a person who is pregnant, or a person in the process of obtaining legal custody of a minor. A landlord cannot refuse to rent to, or impose different terms on, such households absent a valid HOPA exemption.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3602(k) (familial status definition); HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which protected classes were added to the federal Fair Housing Act by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, twenty years after the original 1968 Act?
choice_a: Sex and religion
choice_b: Familial status and disability (handicap)
choice_c: Race and color
choice_d: National origin and age
explanation: The original 1968 Fair Housing Act covered race, color, religion, and national origin; sex was added in 1974. Familial status and disability (handicap) were added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, which also added the design-and-construction accessibility requirements for new multifamily housing.
source_note: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, Pub. L. 100-430; HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, Fair Housing Act history.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The federal agency primarily charged with administering and enforcing the Fair Housing Act, including receiving and investigating discrimination complaints, is the:
choice_a: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
choice_b: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
choice_c: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
choice_d: U.S. Department of Labor
explanation: HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO) administers the Fair Housing Act, investigates complaints, and can refer pattern-or-practice cases to the Department of Justice. The FTC and CFPB play roles in consumer financial protection generally, not primary fair housing enforcement.
source_note: HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (hud.gov/fairhousing).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, discrimination against a person because of race in the sale or rental of a dwelling can be prosecuted with virtually NO available exemptions because of a separate, older civil rights statute. That statute, addressed in the landmark case Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968), is:
choice_a: The Sherman Antitrust Act
choice_b: The Americans with Disabilities Act
choice_c: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act
choice_d: 42 U.S.C. § 1982, guaranteeing all citizens the same right to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property
explanation: In Jones v. Mayer, the U.S. Supreme Court held that 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (derived from the Civil Rights Act of 1866) bars all racial discrimination in the sale or rental of property, private or public, without the exemptions available under the Fair Housing Act. This means the FHA's single-family-home and Mrs. Murphy exemptions never excuse racial discrimination.
source_note: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968); 42 U.S.C. § 1982.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A homeowner who owns three or fewer single-family homes may, in limited circumstances, sell one of those homes without complying with the Fair Housing Act's advertising and conduct rules. Under 42 U.S.C. § 3603, this narrow exemption is immediately lost if the owner:
choice_a: Uses the sales services of a real estate broker, agent, or salesperson, or publishes a discriminatory advertisement
choice_b: Sells the home for more than its assessed value
choice_c: Sells the home to a first-time homebuyer
choice_d: Owns the home for more than five years before selling
explanation: The private-owner exemption applies only if the owner does not use a real estate licensee's services and does not publish any discriminatory notice or advertisement; if a broker is used or discriminatory advertising occurs, the exemption is lost and the Act applies in full.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(1) (Cornell Law School LII).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The so-called "Mrs. Murphy" exemption to the Fair Housing Act applies to:
choice_a: Any rental property with four or fewer bedrooms regardless of occupancy
choice_b: Rooms or units in a dwelling containing living quarters for no more than four families, where the owner occupies one of the units as their residence
choice_c: Commercial retail leases in mixed-use buildings
choice_d: New construction built before the Act's effective date
explanation: The Mrs. Murphy exemption (42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2)) covers owner-occupied dwellings with living quarters for no more than four families, as long as the owner actually maintains and occupies one unit as their own residence. Like the single-family exemption, it never excuses race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 1982, and it doesn't excuse discriminatory advertising.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2) (Cornell Law School LII).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Housing that legitimately qualifies as "housing for older persons" under the Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) is exempt from Fair Housing Act liability for discrimination based on which protected class only?
choice_a: Race
choice_b: Disability
choice_c: Familial status
choice_d: Religion
explanation: HOPA allows qualifying senior communities (e.g., 100% age 62-or-older housing, or 55-or-older housing meeting HUD's occupancy and verification standards, at least 80% of units having one occupant 55+) to exclude families with children without violating the familial status protection. It does not exempt the community from any other protected class, including disability.
source_note: Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, senior housing exemption guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A religious organization that owns rental housing operated for a non-commercial purpose may generally give preference to members of its own religion under the Fair Housing Act, provided that:
choice_a: It is registered as a private club with the state
choice_b: The housing was built after 1988
choice_c: It obtains a HUD waiver in advance
choice_d: Membership in the religion is not restricted based on race, color, or national origin
explanation: The FHA's limited religious-organization exemption allows a preference for co-religionists in non-commercial housing, but only if the religion itself does not restrict membership on the basis of race, color, or national origin. A similar limited exemption exists for bona fide private clubs providing lodging to members as an incident of membership.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3607(a) (religious organization and private club exemptions).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A real estate agent shows homebuyers of one race only listings in certain neighborhoods and actively discourages them from viewing homes in other neighborhoods, while showing buyers of a different race a broader range of listings. This discriminatory practice is known as:
choice_a: Steering
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Blockbusting
choice_d: Tying
explanation: Steering is the practice of directing prospective buyers or renters toward or away from particular neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic, limiting their housing choices. It violates the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discrimination in the terms, conditions, or provision of services related to a sale or rental.
source_note: HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, "Fair Housing: It's Your Right" — definitions of discriminatory housing practices; 42 U.S.C. § 3604.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A licensee tells a homeowner that property values in the neighborhood are about to decline because members of a particular protected class are moving in, urging the owner to sell quickly and below market value. This illegal practice is called:
choice_a: Redlining
choice_b: Blockbusting (panic selling/panic peddling)
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: A group boycott
explanation: Blockbusting, also called panic peddling or panic selling, is inducing owners to sell (often at a below-market price) by suggesting that the entry of persons of a particular protected class into the neighborhood will lower property values or change the neighborhood's character. It is expressly prohibited by the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e); HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity guidance on blockbusting.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A lender systematically refuses to make mortgage loans, or offers less favorable loan terms, in specific neighborhoods based on the racial or ethnic composition of the residents rather than on individual creditworthiness. This practice is known as:
choice_a: Blockbusting
choice_b: Steering
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: Market allocation
explanation: Redlining is the discriminatory practice of denying or limiting financial services (loans, insurance) to residents of certain areas based on the racial or ethnic makeup of those areas, rather than legitimate underwriting criteria. It violates the Fair Housing Act and, in the lending context, also implicates the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Community Reinvestment Act.
source_note: HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity guidance; U.S. Dept. of Justice fair lending / redlining enforcement initiative.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, the difference between a "reasonable accommodation" and a "reasonable modification" for a resident with a disability is best described as:
choice_a: A reasonable accommodation applies only to renters, while a reasonable modification applies only to owners
choice_b: They are two names for the exact same legal requirement with no practical difference
choice_c: A reasonable accommodation must be paid for by the housing provider, while a reasonable modification is never permitted in rental housing
choice_d: A reasonable accommodation is a change in rules, policies, or services; a reasonable modification is a structural or physical change to the dwelling or premises
explanation: A reasonable accommodation is a change in rules, policies, practices, or services (e.g., allowing an assistance animal despite a no-pets policy). A reasonable modification is a structural change to the interior or exterior of the dwelling (e.g., installing a ramp or grab bars). In private housing, the tenant generally bears the cost of a reasonable modification, while the provider typically bears the cost of a reasonable accommodation.
source_note: HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations Under the Fair Housing Act (2004); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Modifications (2008).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements, covered multifamily dwellings of four or more units must include specified accessibility features (accessible common areas, doors wide enough for wheelchairs, reinforced bathroom walls, etc.) if the building was designed and constructed for first occupancy:
choice_a: After March 13, 1991
choice_b: After January 1, 1968
choice_c: After the Americans with Disabilities Act was passed in 1990
choice_d: At any time, regardless of construction date
explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added design-and-construction accessibility requirements for covered multifamily dwellings (buildings with four or more units) first occupied after March 13, 1991. These are separate from, though related in spirit to, ADA accessibility standards.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3); HUD Fair Housing Act Design Manual.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following occupancy policies is generally considered a legitimate, non-discriminatory business practice rather than illegal familial-status discrimination, according to longstanding HUD guidance?
choice_a: A blanket rule prohibiting any household with children from renting a two-bedroom unit
choice_b: A general occupancy standard of two persons per bedroom, applied based on factors such as unit size and configuration
choice_c: Charging families with children a higher security deposit than childless households
choice_d: Requiring families with children to live only on the ground floor of a building
explanation: HUD's 1998 "Keating Memo" guidance recognizes a general occupancy policy of two persons per bedroom as presumptively reasonable (though not an absolute safe harbor), while blanket child-exclusion rules, discriminatory fee structures, and forced floor assignments based on familial status are all illegal.
source_note: HUD General Counsel memorandum on occupancy standards (1998, "Keating Memo"); 42 U.S.C. § 3604.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, an assistance animal that helps a resident with a disability (which may include an emotional support animal, not limited to trained service dogs) must generally be permitted in housing even under a no-pets policy because it is treated as:
choice_a: A tenant improvement requiring landlord pre-approval fees
choice_b: A service animal under Title III of the ADA, which controls all housing decisions
choice_c: A reasonable accommodation, not a "pet"
choice_d: An amenity the landlord may charge a pet deposit for
explanation: Under the FHA, assistance animals (which can include emotional support animals, not just ADA-defined trained service animals) are addressed as a reasonable accommodation request, not as pets, so pet fees/deposits and pet restrictions generally cannot be applied to them. The FHA's definition of assistance animal is broader than the ADA's narrower service-animal definition, which applies to public accommodations, not housing.
source_note: HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Notice FHEO-2020-01, Assessing a Person's Request to Have an Animal as a Reasonable Accommodation.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: HUD's Quid Pro Quo and Hostile Environment Harassment rule (2016) clarifies that under the Fair Housing Act, sexual harassment of a tenant or applicant by a housing provider or its agent is treated as a form of discrimination based on:
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: National origin
choice_c: Disability
choice_d: Sex
explanation: HUD's rule confirms that quid pro quo harassment (conditioning housing benefits on sexual favors) and hostile-environment harassment (unwelcome sexual conduct that interferes with housing) both constitute prohibited discrimination "because of sex" under the Fair Housing Act, and that housing providers can be liable for the discriminatory conduct of their employees and agents.
source_note: HUD Final Rule, Quid Pro Quo and Hostile Environment Harassment, 24 C.F.R. Part 100 (2016).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A person who believes they have experienced housing discrimination may file an administrative complaint with HUD. Under the Fair Housing Act, the deadline for filing that HUD complaint is generally:
choice_a: One year from the date of the alleged discriminatory act
choice_b: 30 days from the date of the alleged discriminatory act
choice_c: Six years from the date of the alleged discriminatory act
choice_d: There is no deadline for filing a HUD complaint
explanation: A HUD administrative complaint generally must be filed within one year of the alleged discriminatory housing practice. A private civil lawsuit in federal or state court, by contrast, generally must be filed within two years of the alleged practice (subject to certain tolling rules).
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3610(a)(1)(A)(i) (HUD complaint deadline) and § 3613(a)(1)(A) (civil action deadline).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: If HUD, after investigating a fair housing complaint, finds reasonable cause that discrimination occurred, either party may elect to have the case decided by a federal administrative law judge, or a party may instead elect to have the case heard by a U.S. District Court. If HUD's own administrative law judge process is used and no election is made, the case is heard by:
choice_a: A jury of the aggrieved party's neighbors
choice_b: A HUD administrative law judge
choice_c: The state real estate commission
choice_d: The Federal Trade Commission
explanation: Absent an election by a party to proceed in federal district court, HUD charges are heard by a HUD administrative law judge, who can award actual damages, injunctive relief, and civil penalties. If any party elects a civil action instead, the U.S. Department of Justice litigates on behalf of the aggrieved party in federal court.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3612 (administrative law judge proceedings) and § 3614 (DOJ civil actions).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The U.S. Department of Justice may independently bring a "pattern or practice" lawsuit under the Fair Housing Act even without a prior individual HUD complaint when:
choice_a: Only after every individual harmed has separately sued in state court
choice_b: Only when the discrimination involves a federally insured lender
choice_c: There is reasonable cause to believe a person or entity is engaged in a pattern or practice of discrimination, or the case raises an issue of general public importance
choice_d: The DOJ has no independent enforcement authority under the Fair Housing Act
explanation: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3614, the Attorney General may file a civil action whenever there is reasonable cause to believe a pattern or practice of discrimination exists, or whenever a group of persons has been denied FHA rights and the case raises an issue of general public importance, independent of any individual HUD complaint.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3614 (pattern-or-practice suits); U.S. Dept. of Justice, Civil Rights Division, Fair Housing Act overview.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: In Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982), the U.S. Supreme Court held that "testers" — individuals who pose as prospective buyers or renters solely to gather evidence of discriminatory practices, without any genuine intent to rent or buy — may still:
choice_a: Never bring a Fair Housing Act claim because they lacked genuine intent to rent
choice_b: Only report violations to HUD but never sue in court
choice_c: Sue only if they are members of the protected class allegedly discriminated against
choice_d: Have legal standing to sue for a Fair Housing Act violation if they were given false information about availability
explanation: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman held that a fair housing tester has standing to sue under the FHA when they are given false information about the availability of housing, because that misinformation itself is an injury under the Act, regardless of the tester's lack of genuine interest in renting.
source_note: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Remedies available for a proven Fair Housing Act violation can include actual damages, injunctive relief, and:
choice_a: Punitive damages in a civil action, without the statutory caps that apply to some other federal civil rights claims
choice_b: Only a formal written apology from the respondent
choice_c: Mandatory revocation of the respondent's real estate license by HUD
choice_d: Criminal imprisonment in every case, regardless of intent
explanation: In a private civil action under the Fair Housing Act, courts may award actual and punitive damages (uncapped by the FHA itself, unlike the tiered caps under Title I of the ADA) plus injunctive or other equitable relief and attorney's fees. HUD administrative proceedings can also impose civil penalties, but license revocation is a state licensing-board matter, not a direct HUD remedy.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c) (private civil action remedies).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is divided into several titles. Which title generally applies to a real estate brokerage's sales or leasing office as a "place of public accommodation"?
choice_a: Title I
choice_b: Title III
choice_c: Title II
choice_d: Title IV
explanation: ADA Title I addresses employment discrimination, Title II covers state and local government services, and Title III covers places of public accommodation, including many real estate sales and leasing offices, which must provide accessible facilities and services to the public. Title IV addresses telecommunications relay services.
source_note: Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.; ADA.gov, ADA Title III Regulations primer.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under ADA Title III, a public accommodation such as a real estate brokerage's office must remove architectural barriers to access when doing so is:
choice_a: Required only if the building was constructed after 2010
choice_b: Required regardless of cost or feasibility
choice_c: "Readily achievable" — that is, easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense
choice_d: Never required for leased office space, only owned space
explanation: ADA Title III requires existing public accommodations to remove architectural barriers when it is "readily achievable" to do so — meaning easily accomplished without much difficulty or expense — considering factors such as cost, resources, and the nature of the business.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 12182(b)(2)(A)(iv); ADA.gov, ADA Title III primer, "readily achievable" barrier removal standard.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the ADA's disability-related coverage from the Fair Housing Act's?
choice_a: The ADA and the FHA cover exactly the same conduct and were both enacted in 1988
choice_b: The ADA applies only to government-owned housing, while the FHA applies only to private housing
choice_c: The FHA does not address disability at all; only the ADA does
choice_d: ADA Title III generally governs accessibility of a real estate office as a place of public accommodation, while the FHA governs disability discrimination in the sale or rental of the dwellings themselves
explanation: ADA Title III addresses accessibility of public accommodations, including a brokerage's or property manager's business premises open to the public, while the Fair Housing Act's disability provisions (added in 1988) address discrimination in housing transactions themselves — refusal to rent/sell, reasonable accommodations/modifications, and design-and-construction standards for covered multifamily housing.
source_note: ADA.gov, ADA Title III primer; Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the ADA, a "service animal" is narrowly defined (generally a dog, in some cases a miniature horse, individually trained to perform tasks for a person with a disability). Compared to the FHA's "assistance animal" standard, the ADA's service-animal definition is:
choice_a: Narrower, and applies to public accommodations rather than housing itself
choice_b: Broader, and applies to housing units rather than public accommodations
choice_c: Identical in scope and legal context
choice_d: Not relevant to real estate in any respect
explanation: The ADA's service-animal definition is narrower (task-trained dogs, and in limited cases miniature horses) and governs access to public accommodations like a leasing office. The FHA's assistance-animal concept is broader, including animals that provide emotional support without specialized training, and governs the resident's dwelling unit as a reasonable accommodation issue.
source_note: ADA Title III regulations, 28 C.F.R. § 36.104; HUD FHEO Notice 2020-01.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Two competing real estate brokers in the same market agree with each other on what commission rate they will each charge sellers. This conduct is a per se violation of the:
choice_a: Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discriminatory terms
choice_b: Sherman Antitrust Act's prohibition on price fixing
choice_c: Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act's anti-kickback provision
choice_d: Truth in Lending Act
explanation: Agreements between competing brokers to fix commission rates, rather than each independently setting its own rates, constitute price fixing, a per se (automatically illegal, with no business-justification defense) violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act (15 U.S.C. § 1).
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1; U.S. Dept. of Justice, Antitrust Division, guidance on real estate brokerage competition.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A group of brokers in a local market agree among themselves to refuse to show properties listed by, or cooperate in any transaction with, a new discount brokerage that charges lower commissions. This coordinated refusal to deal is known as a:
choice_a: Tying arrangement
choice_b: Redlining scheme
choice_c: Group boycott
choice_d: Market allocation agreement
explanation: A group boycott is an agreement among competitors to collectively refuse to deal with another market participant (such as a discount brokerage) in order to disadvantage or exclude it from competing. Like price fixing, group boycotts among competitors are generally treated as per se violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1; U.S. Dept. of Justice/FTC, Antitrust Guidance for real estate professionals.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Two brokerage firms that would otherwise compete agree that one firm will only list and sell properties in the northern part of a city while the other will only operate in the southern part, so that neither competes for the other's customers. This is an illegal antitrust practice known as:
choice_a: Blockbusting
choice_b: Steering
choice_c: A tying arrangement
choice_d: Market allocation
explanation: Market allocation (or customer/territory allocation) occurs when competitors agree to divide markets, territories, or types of customers between themselves instead of competing, eliminating competition that antitrust law is designed to protect. It is treated as a per se Sherman Act violation, just like price fixing and group boycotts.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1; U.S. Dept. of Justice, Antitrust Division, real estate industry guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A brokerage tells a home seller that it will only list the property if the seller also agrees to use the brokerage's affiliated title company and mortgage lender for the transaction. Conditioning one service on the purchase of another, distinct service raises antitrust concerns known as:
choice_a: A tying arrangement
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: Familial status discrimination
explanation: A tying arrangement conditions the sale or availability of one product or service (here, brokerage listing services) on the buyer's purchase of a separate, distinct product or service (title or lending services), potentially violating antitrust law when the seller has sufficient market power in the tying product. In real estate settlement services specifically, similar conduct may also raise anti-kickback concerns under RESPA.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1; U.S. Dept. of Justice, Antitrust Division, tying arrangement guidance.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Individuals or firms found to have violated the Sherman Antitrust Act through price fixing, group boycotts, or market allocation may be subject to which of the following consequences?
choice_a: Only a private letter of reprimand from the local MLS
choice_b: Civil treble damages, injunctive relief, and potential criminal penalties
choice_c: No penalty unless a consumer was individually named as a plaintiff
choice_d: Automatic loss of real estate license with no other consequence
explanation: Sherman Act violations can expose individuals and firms to civil liability for treble (triple) damages plus attorney's fees in private suits, injunctive relief sought by the DOJ or FTC, and criminal prosecution (fines and imprisonment) for the most serious violations such as price fixing and bid rigging.
source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1-2; Clayton Act, 15 U.S.C. § 15 (treble damages).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: HUD's fair housing advertising guidance recommends that print, broadcast, and online real estate advertisements include the Equal Housing Opportunity logo, statement, or slogan primarily in order to:
choice_a: Satisfy a state sales tax disclosure requirement
choice_b: Replace the need for a real estate license number on the ad
choice_c: Communicate that the advertised property is available to all persons regardless of protected class, helping demonstrate a nondiscriminatory advertising policy
choice_d: Guarantee financing approval for all applicants
explanation: The Equal Housing Opportunity (EHO) logo, statement, or slogan signals compliance with fair housing law and a policy of non-discrimination in housing advertising. HUD encourages its consistent use across print, broadcast, and digital/online advertising, including websites and social media listings.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109; HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Under the Fair Housing Act, an advertisement for the sale or rental of a dwelling that states a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class is illegal:
choice_a: Only if a specific complainant can prove they were personally denied housing because of the ad
choice_b: Only if the advertisement appears in a printed newspaper, not online
choice_c: Only if the advertisement uses an explicit racial slur
choice_d: Even if the seller or landlord did not personally intend to discriminate, because the Act prohibits any statement indicating such a preference or limitation
explanation: Section 3604(c) of the Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to make, print, or publish any notice, statement, or advertisement that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, or an intention to make such a preference — regardless of the advertiser's subjective intent, and regardless of the ad's medium (print, broadcast, or online).
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following phrases in a rental listing would most likely be considered a red flag for illegal discriminatory advertising under the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: "Ideal for a mature single professional or couple, no children please"
choice_b: "Spacious two-bedroom apartment with in-unit laundry"
choice_c: "Available immediately, credit and background check required"
choice_d: "Close to public transportation and shopping"
explanation: Phrases like "adults preferred," "no children," or describing a unit as ideal for a certain type of household signal a familial-status preference or limitation and are red flags under HUD advertising guidance, unless the property genuinely and lawfully qualifies for a HOPA senior-housing exemption. Describing amenities, requiring standard screening criteria applied uniformly, and noting proximity to transit are neutral, non-discriminatory statements.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109, Appendix I (illustrative discriminatory terms).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: HUD's fair housing advertising guidance applies to:
choice_a: Only advertisements placed in a local newspaper's classified section
choice_b: All advertising media, including newspapers, radio, television, and internet/social media listings
choice_c: Only advertisements for properties over $1 million in value
choice_d: Only advertisements placed by a licensed broker, never by a private seller
explanation: Fair housing advertising rules apply across all media — print, broadcast, and digital, including websites, social media, and online listing services — and can apply to advertising by private sellers/landlords as well as licensees, since the exemption for private owners is lost entirely if a discriminatory advertisement or notice is published.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109; Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: When choosing photographs of models or actors to depict prospective residents in a real estate advertisement, HUD guidance suggests that a truly nondiscriminatory ad campaign should generally:
choice_a: Include only images of adults without children, regardless of the housing type advertised
choice_b: Avoid using human models altogether in every advertisement
choice_c: Depict a range of persons reflecting diversity across protected classes rather than exclusively one race, family type, or age group
choice_d: Feature only models who match the current resident demographics of the building
explanation: HUD guidance indicates that consistently depicting only one race, family composition, or age group in marketing models/actors can itself signal an unlawful preference, so advertisers are encouraged to use models reflecting the diversity of the broader community to avoid the appearance of a discriminatory preference.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 C.F.R. Part 109 (use of human models).

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property manager acting as an agent for a rental property owner owes the owner fiduciary duties similar to those a real estate broker owes a client, which most importantly includes:
choice_a: Approving every prospective tenant regardless of screening results, to maximize occupancy
choice_b: Setting rental rates without regard to market conditions or the owner's instructions
choice_c: Personally guaranteeing the owner against all vacancy losses
choice_d: Acting in the owner's best financial interest, accounting for funds, and providing accurate financial reporting
explanation: A property manager typically acts as the owner's general agent under a property management agreement, owing fiduciary duties that include loyalty, obedience to lawful instructions, accounting for all funds collected, and providing accurate, timely financial reporting on the property's performance.
source_note: General agency/property management practice principles; IREM (Institute of Real Estate Management) property management fundamentals.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Rents and security deposits collected by a property manager on behalf of an owner must generally be:
choice_a: Deposited into a separate trust or escrow account and never commingled with the property manager's own operating funds
choice_b: Deposited directly into the property manager's personal checking account for convenience
choice_c: Held as cash on the premises until the lease ends
choice_d: Immediately forwarded to the tenant's bank for safekeeping
explanation: Client funds such as rent and security deposits must be kept in a dedicated trust or escrow account, separate from the property manager's or brokerage's own operating funds. Commingling client funds with personal or company operating funds is a serious violation of fiduciary duty and, in most states, a licensing-law violation subject to discipline.
source_note: General trust account/commingling principles applicable to real estate brokerage and property management practice.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: The general legal doctrine requiring a residential landlord to maintain a rental unit in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition throughout the tenancy is known as the:
choice_a: Doctrine of caveat emptor
choice_b: Implied warranty of habitability
choice_c: Rule against perpetuities
choice_d: Statute of frauds
explanation: The implied warranty of habitability requires residential landlords to keep leased premises in a condition fit for human habitation (functioning utilities, structural safety, freedom from serious health/safety hazards) throughout the lease term, regardless of whether the lease expressly says so. Property managers, as the owner's agent, are typically responsible for coordinating the maintenance and repairs needed to satisfy this obligation.
source_note: General landlord-tenant law principle of implied warranty of habitability, recognized in some form in most U.S. jurisdictions.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Which of the following is a typical, core responsibility of a residential property manager acting under a property management agreement?
choice_a: Determining the legal title to the property and resolving boundary disputes with neighboring landowners
choice_b: Setting federal fair housing policy for the jurisdiction
choice_c: Marketing vacancies, screening and selecting qualified tenants, negotiating and enforcing leases, coordinating maintenance, and reporting financial performance to the owner
choice_d: Acting as the tenant's fiduciary rather than the owner's
explanation: A property manager's core duties typically include marketing available units, screening and selecting tenants (using consistent, lawful criteria), negotiating and enforcing lease terms, coordinating maintenance/repairs, and providing the owner with regular financial reports. The property manager is the owner's agent, not the tenant's, and has no independent authority over legal title or public fair housing policy.
source_note: IREM (Institute of Real Estate Management) and NARPM (National Association of Residential Property Managers) property management practice standards.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: A property management agreement between an owner and a management company most closely creates which type of agency relationship?
choice_a: A universal agency, because the manager may do absolutely anything the owner personally could do, without limitation
choice_b: A special agency limited to a single, one-time transaction only
choice_c: No agency relationship at all, since the manager operates independently of the owner
choice_d: A general agency, because the manager is authorized to conduct a range of ongoing business activities on the owner's behalf
explanation: Property management agreements typically create a general agency, authorizing the manager to handle an ongoing range of matters (leasing, maintenance, rent collection) within the scope of the agreement — broader than a special agency (limited to one transaction, as with a typical listing agreement) but not as unlimited as a universal agency.
source_note: General real estate agency law classification (universal, general, and special agency) as applied to property management agreements.

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Federal Law
question: Because leasing and tenant screening are "terms, conditions, or privileges" of a rental under the Fair Housing Act, a property manager screening prospective tenants must:
choice_a: Apply consistent, non-discriminatory screening criteria to all applicants regardless of protected class
choice_b: Apply stricter income requirements to applicants with children to offset perceived risk
choice_c: Decline all applicants who state they use a wheelchair, citing potential building damage
choice_d: Ask only applicants from certain national origins for additional immigration documentation
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discrimination in the "terms, conditions, or privileges" of a rental, and in the provision of services, applies squarely to tenant screening. A property manager must apply the same qualifying criteria (income, credit, rental history, etc.) uniformly to every applicant, regardless of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability.
source_note: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b); HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, tenant screening guidance.
